questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Level Surface
questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)}{{e}^{x-y}},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=-2.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)}{{e}^{x-y}} & =-2 \\ z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =-2{e}^{x-y} \\ z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=-2$ is the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2{e}^{x-y}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Level Surface
questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =1 \\ 2z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ z & =\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=1$ is the paraboloid $z=\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z,$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=0.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ 9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z & =0 \\ z & =9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ z & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{1/9}+{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=0$ is the elliptic paraboloid $z=\frac{{x}^{2}}{1/9}+{y}^{2}.$

questions.worked_solution:

questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Describing a Level Surface of a Function
questions.problem: Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡z}{x+y}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡z}{x+y} & =c \\ \operatorname{arcsin}⁡z & =c(x+y) \\ z & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(c(x+y))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get a family of surfaces given by:

$$
z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(c(x+y)),\,c\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

choices.value: A family of surfaces given by $z=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(c(x+y))$
A family of surfaces given by $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(c(x+y))$
A family of surfaces given by $z=c\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)$
A family of surfaces given by $z=\operatorname{cos}⁡(c(x+y))$

answer_fields.correct_value: A family of surfaces given by $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(c(x+y))$

questions.knowledge_point: Describing a Level Surface of a Function
questions.problem: Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {e}^{-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}} & =c \\ -{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡c \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡c\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $0<c\le 1$ since $-\operatorname{ln}⁡c$ must be non-negative. If we let $-\operatorname{ln}⁡c={r}^{2},$ we get

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}={r}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the level surfaces form a family of spheres centered at the origin.

choices.value: A family of surfaces given by  ${z}^{2}+c={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ for $c>0$
A family of spheres centered at $(0,0,e)$
A family of spheres centered at $(0,0,{e}^{-1})$
A family of spheres centered at the origin
A family of surfaces given by ${z}^{2}+c={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ for $c\ne 0$

answer_fields.correct_value: A family of spheres centered at the origin

questions.knowledge_point: Describing a Level Surface of a Function
questions.problem: Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡z?$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡z & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-c \\ z & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-c}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get a family of curves:

$$
z={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-c},\,c\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

mathematical_assessment.explanation: Recomputing f=c gives ln(z)=x²+y²−c and therefore z=e^{x²+y²−c}. Only option d has this equation. The earlier uncertainty remains because d calls these surfaces 'curves': each fixed c gives a two-dimensional graph over all (x,y). Thus no displayed description is fully correct, although d matches the calculation.

questions.problem: Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{3z}{x+6y}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{3z}{x+6y} & =c \\ 3z & =c(x+6y) \\ 3z & =cx+6cy \\ z & =\frac{c}{3}x+2cy\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get a family of planes:

$$
z=\frac{c}{3}x+2cy,\,c\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z+2?$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z+2 & =c \\ z & ={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2-c\end{aligned}
$$

If we let $2-c=C,$ we get a family of hyperbolic paraboloids:

$$
z={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+C,\,c\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

choices.value: A family of hyperboloids of one sheet: ${z}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}={C}^{2}$
A family of hyperboloids of two sheets: ${z}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}=-{C}^{2}$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Level Surface of a Function Passing Through a Point
questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=2x-3{y}^{2}+z$ that passes through the point $P(1,1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,1) & =2(1)-3({1}^{2})+1 \\  & =2-3+1 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ 2x-3{y}^{2}+z & =0 \\ z & =3{y}^{2}-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,1,1)$ is the surface $z=3{y}^{2}-2x.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Level Surface of a Function Passing Through a Point
questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)-\sqrt{xy}$ that passes through the point $P(1,1,e).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,e) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot e)-\sqrt{1\cdot 1}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=0.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)-\sqrt{xy} & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz) & =\sqrt{xy} \\ xyz & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}} \\ z & =\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,1,e)$ is the surface $z=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{xy}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Level Surface of a Function Passing Through a Point
questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}$ that passes through the point $P(1,0,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,-1) & =\frac{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{1} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{z}^{2}} & =1 \\ {z}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,0,-1)$ is the cone ${z}^{2}={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=x-2y+z$ that passes through the point $P(1,1,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,-1) & =1-2(1)+(-1) \\  & =1-2-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=-2.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ x-2y+z & =-2 \\ x-2y+z+2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,1,-1)$ is the plane $x-2y+z+2=0.$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{z-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{xy}$ that passes through the point $P(1,1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,2) & =\frac{(2)-(1)^{2}+(1)^{2}}{(1)(1)}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=2.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{z-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{xy} & =2 \\ z-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2xy \\ z & ={x}^{2}+2xy-{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,1,2)$ is the surface $z={x}^{2}+2xy-{y}^{2}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Level Surface
canonical_examples.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z) = x^2+4y^2-z,$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z) = c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c = 0.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-z & =0 \\ z & ={x}^{2}+4{y}^{2} \\ z & ={x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{1/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=0$ is the elliptic paraboloid $z = x^2+\dfrac{y^2}{{1/4}}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Describing a Level Surface of a Function
canonical_examples.problem: Find the family of surfaces that describe the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y, z) = \ln(x^2 + 2y^2 - z^2).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & ={e}^{c} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{e}^{c}}+\frac{2{y}^{2}}{{e}^{c}}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{{e}^{c}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get a family of hyperboloids of one sheet:

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{e^c} + \dfrac{y^2}{e^c/2} - \dfrac{z^2}{e^c} =  1, \qquad c \in (-\infty,\infty)
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Level Surface of a Function Passing Through a Point
canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z) = \sin{xyz}$ that passes through the point $P\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
  f\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&= \sin \left(\pi\cdot 1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sin{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} = 1}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z) = c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c = 1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡xyz & =1 \\ xyz & =\frac{\pi }{2}+2\pi k\end{aligned}
$$

where $k$ is any integer.

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is the surface $xyz= \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi k,$ where $k$ is any integer.
